title: Riverbed, Shrine Gate and Hillside: Higashiyama and the Kamo River
standfirst: Between the Kamo River and the Higashiyama hills lies ground that was once open riverbed, shrine land and the road to a burial field. Embankments turned it into Gion's teahouse streets, a flood in 1935 remade the river, and war erased one street while sparing the rest. This dossier shows how to read those layers today.

sections.heading: A river the emperors could not command

paragraphs.text: The Kamo River rises in the mountains north of Kyoto, enters the basin at Kamigamo, meets the Takano River near Demachi and runs for about 23 km down the eastern side of the city, picking up the Shirakawa stream near Shijo before it joins the Katsura at Shimotoba. A prefectural gazetteer of 1915 describes a bed of sand and gravel carrying shallow, clear water against the green screen of the Higashiyama hills. What no one could tame was the flood. The Tale of the Heike has the retired emperor Shirakawa name the waters of the Kamo first among the three things he could not control, ahead of the dice of the sugoroku board and the warrior monks of Mount Hiei.

The court set up an office to guard against the river, the Bokashi (防鴨河使), in 824, but Kyoto City's historians judge that it achieved little: in a flood of 1017 the city east of Tominokoji became a sea and about 300 patients of the Hiden-in charity hospital were swept away. Until the seventeenth century the Kamo was a natural river with wide flats of stones on either bank. In 1669 work began on new stone embankments, finished the following year. This Kanbun embankment (寛文新堤) fixed the channel, the flats behind it were built over, and the riverside townscape that visitors now take for granted was born.

sections.heading: Shrine land and the road to Kiyomizu

paragraphs.text: East of the river the ground rises through the precinct of the Gion shrine, called Gion-sha or Gion Kanshin-in until 1868 and Yasaka Shrine since. The shrine keeps two founding traditions: that in 656 a man named Irishi, who had come from Koma (the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo), enshrined here Susanoo, the god of Mount Gozu in Silla; and that the Nara monk Ennyo built a hall on the spot in 876. A government decree of 1070 in the shrine's archives set its domain as the land between the hills and the Kamo, from Sanjo south to old Gojo, today's Matsubara-dori, which is roughly the northern half of the area covered by this dossier. By the shrine's account the Gion festival began in 869, when an epidemic was answered with 66 halberds, one for each province, and the shrine's portable shrine was carried to the imperial garden of Shinsen-en.

South of the shrine the district was a threshold. Rokuhara, between old Gojo and Shichijo, was the way into Toribeno, the burial ground on the slopes, and was imagined as the border between this world and the next. Kuya founded the temple that became Rokuharamitsuji in 963; in the twelfth century the Taira clan filled Rokuhara with their mansions, and burned them when they fled the capital in 1183. The same lanes were the pilgrim road to Kiyomizu-dera, which a late-Heian song collection maps stop by stop from the stone bridge at Gojo. Kiyomizu-dera dates its founding to 778, beside the spring that still falls as the Otowa waterfall; most of its present halls, including the main hall with its famous stage over the slope, were rebuilt in 1633.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi reshaped the southern half. From 1586 he raised a Great Buddha hall about 49 m high just south of today's Gojo-dori; its precinct took in the present Hokoji, Toyokuni Shrine and Kyoto National Museum, whose west side still shows the colossal stone walls. The gazetteer of 1915 records that in the Tensho era he moved the Gojo bridge south from Matsubara to its present line, so that the street now called Gojo runs where the old Rokujo-bomon lane ran. In 1597 a mound, which today stands west of Toyokuni Shrine, was raised to bury the noses and ears cut from Korean soldiers and civilians during his invasions of Korea and brought back as trophies; first called the nose mound, it is known as Mimizuka (耳塚). The bell whose inscription Tokugawa Ieyasu used in 1614 as a pretext for the war that destroyed the Toyotomi still hangs at Hokoji.

A city guide of 1928 describes the land between Shijo bridge and the Gion shrine, after the medieval wars, as a poor hamlet of scattered farmhouses. From the early Edo period, through the seventeenth century and into the eighteenth, its fields were laid out as streets; tea stalls opened for pilgrims to Gion and Kiyomizu, and in time became restaurants and houses of entertainment. Kyoto City's preservation plan for Gion Shinbashi ties that growth to the Kamo embankment, which pushed the city east across the river, and dates the teahouse streets of Gion's 'inner six blocks' to 1712. According to the 1915 gazetteer, residents won licenses for thirty teahouses in 1732 in return for paying to rebuild the Yamato bridge, which it treats as the beginning of Gion's licensed quarter.

The theater came first. Kabuki began, the 1928 guide says, with performances beside the south gate of the Gion shrine that moved on to the Shijo riverbed. The gazetteer records that seven licensed theaters were permitted on Shijo in 1669, the same year the embankment work began; by the Meiji Restoration two were left, and when the northern one burned the Minamiza (南座) remained alone. West of the river, the merchant Suminokura Ryoi and his son opened the Takase canal in 1614, carrying firewood, rice and sake from Fushimi in flat-bottomed boats about 13 m long until the canal closed in 1920.

The hillside developed its own trades. Kyoto City's plan for Sannenzaka describes a gate town for Kiyomizu-dera, Hokan-ji (the Yasaka pagoda) and the Gion shrine, whose houses spread from the mid-Edo period along the paths linking the temples; its tea shops and craft stores continue the business of early-modern sightseeing. The 1928 guide offers two stories for the slope's name: a hall at Kiyomizu for safe childbirth (産寧, sannei), or a road opened in 808, the third year of Daido. It also notes that Gojo-zaka was lined with pottery shops and the workshops of the best Kiyomizu-ware potters, while Kiyomizu-zaka sold ceramic dolls and sake cups to visitors from the provinces.

sections.heading: Iron bridges, a canal and a railway

paragraphs.text: In 1868 the new government's separation of Shinto and Buddhism turned Gion-sha into Yasaka Shrine. Its Buddhist images went to nearby temples and Buddhist names were removed, although the old name Kanshin-in is still cut into the stone basin just inside the west gate. The pleasure quarter, by then in decline, reinvented itself: for the Kyoto Exhibition of 1872 the owner of the Ichiriki teahouse and the dance teachers devised a new dance, first staged that March in a borrowed hall, and in 1873 it moved to a new dance hall built on Hanamikoji under the name Miyako Odori. By 1915 the gazetteer could report that the dance was known in Europe and America as the 'Cherry Dance'.

The bridges modernised first. Residents of the ward paid for an iron Shijo bridge in April 1874; when the city laid tram tracks it was rebuilt as five reinforced-concrete arches, four over the Kamo and one over the canal, in works completed in 1913. The Lake Biwa Canal reached Kyoto in 1890 and its Kamo extension, running down the east bank to Fushimi through eight locks, was finished in 1894. From 1910 the Keihan railway from Osaka ended at Gojo, and in 1915 it was extended to Sanjo, squeezed between the canal and the river. The 1915 gazetteer judged that the Kamo, once the scourge of the capital, now rarely harmed the city because 'flood control is in place'.

Twenty years later the river answered. A pamphlet published by Kyoto Prefecture in 1935 records four bursts of rain of about 40 mm an hour between 11 p.m. on 28 June and 8 a.m. the next morning; the Kyoto observatory measured 269.9 mm for the day, far above the previous record of 161.3 mm set on 20 August 1900. By 5 a.m. houses around Shijo bridge stood in a meter of water and by 7.30 a.m. in 1.5 m. Driftwood jammed under the Shijo and Shichijo bridges, and in Pontocho and Shichijo Sannocho the water rose more than 2 m above the floors. Soldiers, firemen and youth groups worked through the night to hold the Kamo embankment upstream; had it broken, the pamphlet says, almost the whole city would have become a sea of mud.

Of fifty bridges over the Kamo and Takano inside the city, 35 road bridges and one railway bridge fell, the Sanjo and Gojo bridges among them; only ten came through undamaged, and the mud took more than a month to clear. Kyoto Prefecture's figures today for the Kamo alone are 12 dead or injured, 137 houses washed away and 24,173 flooded; counting the other rivers, 83 people were killed or injured across the city. The Keihan terminus at Sanjo, caught between the canal and the torrent, was badly damaged.

The pamphlet set out a remedy: widen the channel to about 70 m, dig the bed 1 to 3 m deeper to pass 650 cubic meters a second at Shijo, rebuild the banks in stone, and put the Keihan tracks underground beneath the canal with a road on top, removing what it called a 'cancer' on the city's growth. The prefecture carried out the river works from 1936 to 1947, lowering the bed by about 2 m on average, and reports that they brought the Kamo to a standard that carried the flood of August 1959, whose rainfall exceeded that of 1935, without flooding the city. The railway half of the plan had to wait half a century.

sections.heading: War: a spared city and an erased street

paragraphs.text: Kyoto is often said to have escaped the war; a 2014 study of its wartime demolitions calls it a 'non-war-damaged city'. It was not untouched. On the night of 16 January 1945 American bombs fell on Umamachi in Higashiyama, killing more than thirty people. It was Kyoto's first air raid, and with the Nishijin raid of 26 June it is how the city remembers its war. The poet Yoshii Isamu, living two kilometers to the north, noted in his diary that he was told the bombs had fallen 'at Gojo-zaka', that there had been nine of them and about thirty dead, and a few days later that many people in Higashiyama were leaving.

The greater loss was planned. Although Kyoto was not designated an evacuation zone, from 1944 it demolished houses for firebreaks in four rounds. The third, in March and April 1945, cleared belts along Horikawa, Oike and Gojo and around Kyoto Station: 140 sites, 120 hectares and 10,475 houses, according to a 2007 historical atlas summarised by the Itami City Library, opened into strips 50 to 100 m wide. On Horikawa, notices went up from 18 March and demolition began around 25 March. After the war about half of the cleared land was bought for roads and parks and the rest was returned; Oike-dori, cleared in the same campaign, was fixed as a 50-meter planning road in 1947.

The 1945-1950 aerial photograph in this dossier shows both outcomes. The roofs of Gion, Miyagawa-cho and the Kiyomizu slopes are dense and whole, and the Kamo's gravel bars and the east-bank line of canal and railway are sharp, but a pale, broken band runs east from Gojo bridge where the houses of Gojo-dori had been pulled down. Today the same line is a multi-lane road; set the two photographs side by side and the scale of the 1945 demolitions is plain.

Two decisions of 1976 fixed parts of the old landscape. On 1 July that year Kyoto City declared Sannenzaka and Gion Shinbashi historic preservation districts, moving them from a townscape scheme of its own, begun in 1972, into the new national system; Ishibe-koji was added to the Sannenzaka district in 1995. About seven in ten of Shinbashi's roughly 75 buildings are traditional teahouse-style townhouses, some with back rooms over the Shirakawa, and about 65 percent of the buildings in the Sannenzaka district are traditional, from mushiko-style townhouses with low upper floors to Taisho-era houses on Ishibe-koji.

The railway half of the 1935 plan came true on 24 May 1987, when the Keihan line between Tofukuji and Sanjo went underground. The city built Kawabata-dori on the old track bed, removing eight level crossings that had knotted the traffic on Shijo and Gojo. The broad road on the east bank is therefore the railway's former route, and the deepened channel below it dates from the works of 1936-1947.

Smaller traces reward a closer look. Under Sanjo Ohashi, stone piers said to date from Hideyoshi's bridge stand on concrete footings added when the bed was lowered; under Shijo Ohashi, timber piles from the arched bridge of 1913 still break the surface. Gojo-dori, much wider than the old streets around it, is the firebreak of 1945. And on Shijo-dori east of Yamato-oji the small temple Chugen-ji keeps a Jizo said to have been enshrined after the river commissioner Seta Tamekane checked a flood in 1228: the 'rain-stopping Jizo', whose name drifted over the centuries into the 'eye-disease Jizo'.

timeline.what: The court creates the Bokashi, an office to repair the Kamo embankments.
Gion goryo-e, the rite against epidemic that became the Gion Festival, according to Yasaka Shrine.
A government decree fixes the Gion shrine's domain between the hills, the Kamo, Sanjo and old Gojo.
Sanjo Ohashi built under Hideyoshi by Mashita Nagamori; in the same Tensho era the Gojo bridge is moved south from Matsubara.
Mimizuka raised beside the Great Buddha hall of Hokoji.
Kanbun stone embankments built along the Kamo; seven theaters licensed on Shijo (1669).
Teahouse streets of Gion's 'inner six blocks', today's Shinbashi district, laid out.
Gion-sha renamed Yasaka Shrine under the separation of Shinto and Buddhism.
Kamo canal of the Lake Biwa Canal completed along the east bank.
Keihan railway opens to Gojo (1910) and Sanjo (1915) along the east bank.
Record rain floods the Kamo; Sanjo and Gojo bridges are washed away. River works follow, 1936-1947.
16 January: Umamachi air raid. March-April: houses along Gojo, Horikawa and Oike demolished for firebreaks.
Sannenzaka and Gion Shinbashi become historic preservation districts (1 July).
Keihan line put underground between Tofukuji and Sanjo; Kawabata-dori built on the track bed.

walk.name: Sanjo Ohashi
walk.what: From the riverbank path, look at the piers: stone columns said to survive from Hideyoshi's bridge of 1590 now stand on concrete footings, added when the riverbed was lowered by about 2 m after the 1935 flood. The bronze finials (giboshi) on the railings were already treasured in 1915 as relics of that bridge.

walk.name: Shijo Ohashi, Minamiza and Chugen-ji
walk.ja: 四条大橋・南座・仲源寺（目疾地蔵）
walk.what: Under the bridge, look for the timber piles of the 1913 arch bridge; at its east end stands the Minamiza, the last of the Shijo theaters licensed in 1669. A short walk east along Shijo-dori, past Yamato-oji, Chugen-ji keeps the flood-stopping Jizo of 1228.

walk.name: Gion Shinbashi and the Shirakawa
walk.what: The teahouse street of 1712, with two-storey townhouses whose back rooms overhang the Shirakawa; stone paving and willows are protected with the buildings.

walk.name: Yasaka Shrine, west gate
walk.what: The west gate closes the eastern end of Shijo-dori. Just inside it, on the left, find the old name Kanshin-in cut into the stone water basin, a survivor of the renaming of 1868.

walk.name: Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka to Kiyomizu-dera
walk.ja: 産寧坂・二年坂・清水寺
walk.what: Stone steps and bent lanes of the 1976 preservation district lead past the Yasaka pagoda to the temple of 778 and its stage over the slope.

walk.name: Gojo-zaka down to Gojo Ohashi
walk.what: Pottery shops recall the Kiyomizu-ware trade described in 1928. Walking down to the river, note the breadth of Gojo-dori: the firebreak of spring 1945. The bridge itself stands on the line to which Hideyoshi moved it.

walk.name: Hokoji bell and Mimizuka
walk.what: South of Gojo, the stone walls of the Great Buddha precinct run beside the National Museum; the bell of 1614 hangs at Hokoji, and west of Toyokuni Shrine the mound of Mimizuka, topped by a stone stupa, marks where the trophies taken in the invasions of Korea were buried.

deepResearchLeads.how: Read online (NDL) or ask Yasaka Shrine's office about access to originals.

caveats: Sources date the Kanbun embankment slightly differently: Kyoto City's historical archives give 1669-1670 for stone banks on both sides, while a Kyoto Prefecture column gives 1668 for the right bank between Imadegawa and Gojo.

Founding dates for Yasaka Shrine (656 or 876) and Kiyomizu-dera (778) are institutional traditions, reported here as such. The 1915 prefectural gazetteer gives 869 for the shrine's founding and 876 for the first goryo-e, the reverse of the shrine's own account followed here.

Casualty figures for the 1935 flood and the Umamachi raid differ between sources; this dossier gives Kyoto Prefecture's current flood figures and the Prefectural Library's 'more than thirty' for Umamachi.
The observations on the 1945-1950 photograph were made on the GSI tiles at zoom 16; features smaller than a house plot cannot be read reliably at that scale.
